subject: Critical Thinking
title: Lincoln-Douglas Debate: Values in Conflict
description: A quick, practical guide to Lincoln-Douglas Debate: Values in Conflict.

hook.text: 1858: Abraham Lincoln & Stephen Douglas debated slavery across seven Illinois towns.

buildup.text: Lincoln-Douglas format: a one-on-one values debate.

discovery.text: LD requires a 'value criterion': the standard by which the debate is judged.

twist.text: The format forces philosophical depth. You can't win with just facts — you must argue about what MATTERS and why.

climax.text: Modern LD debate trains Supreme Court clerks, policy makers, & ethicists.

punchline.text: Facts tell you what IS. Values tell you what SHOULD be. Both need arguments.

quiz.question: What makes Lincoln-Douglas debate different from other formats?
options: It's a one-on-one values debate focused on philosophical and moral reasoning
It requires three people per team

details.summary: Lincoln-Douglas debate pits two competing values against each other, forcing debaters to argue which matters more in a given context. It trains you to reason about moral trade-offs rather than just facts.
details.whyItMatters: Most real-world dilemmas are not about facts but about which values should take priority. LD debate develops the skill of weighing competing goods.
takeaways: LD debate centers on value conflicts, not factual disputes
Debaters must define and defend a value criterion
It mirrors real ethical decision-making under constraint

faq.question: How does Lincoln-Douglas debate differ from policy debate?
faq.answer: Policy debate focuses on specific plans and their consequences. Lincoln-Douglas centers on abstract value conflicts: should security or liberty prevail? It trains moral reasoning rather than policy analysis.

faq.question: What is a value criterion in Lincoln-Douglas debate?
faq.answer: The value criterion is the standard used to measure which value better achieves the resolution's goal. It provides a framework for judges and opponents to evaluate competing moral claims.
